evidence: CreateTaskUseCase.ts: private generateId() returns `task_${Date.now()}_${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2)}`. Same ID format defined a second time.
AssignTaskUseCase.ts execute(): `new Task(task.id, task.projectId, task.title, task.description, task.status, task.dueDate, userId)` rebuilds the entity instead of calling an entity method.
MarkTaskAsDoneUseCase.ts execute(): `task.markAsDone()` changes state through the entity, unlike AssignTaskUseCase.
CreateTaskUseCase.ts execute(): `new Task(id, dto.projectId, dto.title, dto.description, 'todo', dueDate, null)` hard-codes the starting status and assignee.
AssignTaskUseCase.ts and MarkTaskAsDoneUseCase.ts both repeat `findById(taskId)` + `throw new Error('Task not found')`.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The five files share one concern: project and task use cases. But the module defines the same ID-generation rule in two places and is inconsistent about using the domain entity. AssignTaskUseCase rebuilds a Task through its full constructor to change the assignee. MarkTaskAsDoneUseCase uses the entity's own method (task.markAsDone()). So one use case goes around the entity's behavior while another uses it. CreateTaskUseCase also hard-codes the starting status 'todo' and null assignee, which is an entity rule placed in the use case. The 'Task not found' lookup-and-throw check is also repeated in two files. These match the rubric's fail criteria: a rule defined in more than one place and the module's own abstractions bypassed. Confidence is moderate because the Task entity's source wasn't provided, so I can't confirm whether it already has an assign method.

violations.message: The private generateId() repeats the ID-generation rule also defined in CreateTaskUseCase.generateId(). The rule should live in one shared ID generator.

The private generateId() repeats the ID-generation rule from CreateProjectUseCase. Also, execute() hard-codes the starting status 'todo' and null assignee in `new Task(...)`. These are entity rules that belong in a domain factory.

execute() rebuilds the Task through its full constructor to change the assignee instead of calling an entity method. This goes around the entity's behavior and is inconsistent with MarkTaskAsDoneUseCase's use of task.markAsDone().
